solution: The substitution $u=x^{2}$ is not one-one on $[-1,3]$; it is monotonic on $[-1,0]$ and on $[0,3]$ separately
Total $=\frac14+\frac{9}{20}=\frac{7}{10}$ (one substitution over the whole interval would give the wrong value $0.20$)
solution_full: The natural substitution is $u=x^{2}$, but on $[-1,3]$ the map $x\mapsto x^{2}$ is not monotonic (it decreases on $[-1,0]$ and increases on $[0,3]$), and $|x|\,dx$ equals $\frac12du$ only where $x\ge0$. So split at $0$.

On $[-1,0]$: $|x|=-x$. With $u=x^{2}$, $du=2x\,dx$, so $-x\,dx=-\frac12du$; $x=-1\mapsto u=1$, $x=0\mapsto u=0$. Hence $\int_{-1}^{0}\dfrac{-x}{(1+x^{2})^{2}}dx=-\dfrac12\int_{1}^{0}\dfrac{du}{(1+u)^{2}}=\dfrac12\int_0^{1}\dfrac{du}{(1+u)^{2}}=\dfrac12\left(1-\dfrac12\right)=\dfrac14$.
A single substitution $u=x^{2}$ from $u=1$ to $u=9$ would give $\frac12\left(\frac12-\frac1{10}\right)=0.20$, which is wrong because it treats $|x|\,dx$ as $\frac12du$ on $[-1,0]$ too.
originality_note: New: an integrand whose natural substitution u = x^2 looks valid over the whole interval but is not one-one there, so the limits must be changed piecewise (way 5). Closest known: int_{-1}^{2} x^2 dx with t = x^2 as a textbook warning. Different because: the modulus makes the single substitution produce a plausible wrong value 0.20.
blueprint_concepts: Substitution in a definite integral: changing limits and the monotonicity requirement

concept_use.Substitution in a definite integral: cha: u = x^2 is monotonic only on [-1,0] and [0,3] separately; limits change to [0,1] and [0,9] on the two pieces.

key_step: Split at 0 so that u = x^2 is monotonic, then change limits on each piece.
justification: Routine chain: notice the non-monotonic substitution, two substitutions with changed limits, add. Same demand as 2021-P1-Q2 (L2) in length; no insight beyond splitting.
